title: Phrasal Verbs in Context
story_context: Ahmed is one month into his supervisor role. During his first week, he had to navigate several team conversations using natural English — bringing up issues, following up with colleagues, and sorting out problems. He didn't realize how many phrasal verbs he was already using. This lesson identifies the eight most essential ones, groups them so they're easy to remember, and gives Ahmed the tools to use them confidently in any professional conversation.
objectives: Understand and use 8 essential professional phrasal verbs
Distinguish separable from inseparable phrasal verbs
Group phrasal verbs by theme: problem-solving and professional workflow
Use phrasal verbs naturally in workplace conversations
target_phrases: Can you go over this report with me?
Let's sort out the scheduling issue.
I need to follow up with the client.
Please fill out this form before Friday.
Let's set up a time to meet.
I'd like to bring up a concern.
I'm trying to figure out the problem.

dialogue.title: Ahmed's First Week as Supervisor
dialogue.context: Ahmed has just been promoted to supervisor. During his first week, natural conversations with his team are full of phrasal verbs — words and particles that work together to create new meanings.

lines.speaker: Team Member (Marcus)
lines.text: Ahmed, I wanted to bring up something before our meeting starts. There's a scheduling conflict on Thursday.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Thanks, Marcus. Let's sort that out now. Can you find out what the conflict is exactly?

lines.speaker: Marcus
lines.text: Rosa is taking over the Thursday shift from Carlos, but the new inventory system isn't set up yet.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Okay. I'll go over the setup checklist today and figure out what's missing. Can you follow up with IT?

lines.speaker: Marcus
lines.text: Sure. Should I put off the Thursday handover until the system is ready?

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: No, let's not put it off. Rosa, can you show up 30 minutes early on Thursday so we can go over the process together?

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Of course. I also need to hand in my timesheet — is there a form I need to fill out?

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Yes, fill out the blue form at the front desk. I'll look it up in the employee handbook if you're not sure which one.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Got it. Also, do I get along with everyone on the Thursday team? I don't know all of them.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: You'll be fine — they're great to work with. Just carry out your normal duties and introduce yourself. If any problems come up, bring them up with me right away.

lines.speaker: Marcus
lines.text: Should I set up a quick team meeting so everyone can get to know Rosa?

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Good idea. Set it up for Wednesday afternoon. And Marcus — I appreciate you bringing this up early. It's much easier to sort out problems before they become crises.

pattern_drills.focus: Separable phrasal verbs: fill out, set up, figure out, bring up, sort out
pattern_drills.pattern: SEPARABLE: verb + object + particle OR verb + particle + object. When object is a pronoun, it MUST go in the middle.
examples: fill out the form → fill the form out → fill it out ✓ (NOT: fill out it ✗)
set up the meeting → set the meeting up → set it up ✓
bring up the issue → bring the issue up → bring it up ✓
sort out the problem → sort the problem out → sort it out ✓
figure out the cause → figure the cause out → figure it out ✓
pattern_drills.your_turn: Say: 'Can you set up a meeting? I need to bring up something important.'

prompts.sentence: Please fill ___ the form before leaving.
Can you set ___ a meeting for Thursday afternoon?
Let's sort ___ the scheduling problem before Monday.

pattern_drills.focus: Inseparable phrasal verbs: go over, find out, follow up
pattern_drills.pattern: INSEPARABLE: verb + particle + object (cannot split). Even pronouns come after the whole phrasal verb.
examples: go over the report → go over it ✓ (NOT: go it over ✗)
find out the reason → find out about it ✓ (NOT: find it out ✗ — find out is inseparable)
follow up with the client → follow up with them ✓ (intransitive — object follows the preposition)
Let's go over the checklist before we begin. (always together)
I need to find out why the delivery was late. (inseparable before a clause)
pattern_drills.your_turn: Say: 'I'll go over the report and follow up with you tomorrow.'

prompts.sentence: Let's go ___ the checklist before we start work.
I need to find ___ why the shipment was delayed.
She said she would follow ___ with the supplier.

pattern_drills.focus: 8 core professional phrasal verbs in context
pattern_drills.pattern: Theme 1 — Problem-solving: sort out, find out, figure out, go over | Theme 2 — Workflow: bring up, follow up, set up, fill out
examples: sort out — We need to sort out the scheduling conflict before Thursday. (resolve/organize)
find out — I'll find out when the new shipment is expected. (discover information)
figure out — I'm trying to figure out why the numbers don't match. (understand/solve by thinking)
go over — Let's go over the safety checklist together before we start. (review carefully)
bring up — Please bring up any concerns at the start of the meeting. (raise/mention a topic)
follow up — I'll follow up with the client tomorrow if we don't hear back. (contact again to check)
set up — Can you set up a meeting for Thursday? (arrange/organize)
fill out — You need to fill out this form to request time off. (complete a document)
pattern_drills.your_turn: Use three of these eight phrasal verbs in sentences about a real situation at work or school.

prompts.sentence: I need to ___ out why the numbers don't match. (understand/solve)
She said she would ___ up with the supplier by Friday.
Let's ___ up a call to go over the report together.

listening_exercises.transcript: Phrasal verbs combine a base verb with one or two particles — prepositions or adverbs — to create a new meaning. For example, 'give up' has nothing to do with 'giving' or 'up' literally — it means to stop trying. Many phrasal verbs are separable: the object can come between the verb and particle. 'Fill out the form' and 'fill the form out' are both correct. But pronouns must go in the middle: 'fill it out', not 'fill out it'. Inseparable phrasal verbs cannot be split: 'look after the children', never 'look the children after'.
listening_exercises.question: Where must pronouns go with separable phrasal verbs?

listening_exercises.transcript: Why are phrasal verbs so common in English? They developed from Old English and Germanic roots, making them feel natural and informal compared to their Latin-based equivalents. 'Put off' sounds more casual than 'postpone'. 'Find out' is more conversational than 'discover'. In professional American settings, phrasal verbs appear constantly in spoken language and emails. Learning phrasal verbs helps you sound natural rather than overly formal, and they appear frequently in meetings, presentations, and workplace conversations.
listening_exercises.question: Why do phrasal verbs feel more casual than their equivalents?
options: They come from Old English/Germanic roots, while alternatives are Latin-based
They are used only in conversation

listening_exercises.transcript: Some common particles and their general meanings: 'up' often suggests completion or improvement — finish up, clean up, set up. 'Out' suggests discovery, distribution, or completion — find out, hand out, carry out. 'Over' suggests review or repetition — go over, think over, look over. 'Off' suggests delay or departure — put off, take off, set off. These patterns aren't rules — they're tendencies. The best way to learn phrasal verbs is in context, through reading and listening to real English, noting how each one is used.
listening_exercises.question: What does the particle 'up' often suggest?

speaking_tasks.prompt: Describe your typical workday or school day using as many phrasal verbs from this lesson as you can (aim for 6+). Record for 40 seconds.
speaking_tasks.example: Let me tell you about a typical day as a supervisor. I show up at 7am and first go over the overnight reports to find out if anything needs attention. Then I set up the morning briefing for the team. During the meeting, I bring up any issues from the previous day and we figure out solutions together. I follow up with suppliers who haven't responded, and I fill out any required daily forms before lunch. In the afternoon, I sort out any problems that come up. I hand in my own supervisor report before leaving, and I never put off things that need to be done today.
sentence_starters: First, I show up at ... and go over ...
During [the meeting / my shift], I bring up ... and sort out ...
I always follow up with ... and never put off ...

speaking_tasks.prompt: A new employee is starting tomorrow. Give them 5 pieces of advice using phrasal verbs. For each one, explain what the phrasal verb means. Record for 35 seconds.
speaking_tasks.example: Welcome advice for your first day. First, show up five minutes early — that means arrive before your scheduled start time, not exactly on time. Second, go over any training materials the night before — that means review them carefully. Third, don't put off questions — ask right away if you're unsure about something; putting it off means delaying. Fourth, try to get along with everyone — having good relationships is essential here. Fifth, if a problem comes up, bring it up with your supervisor immediately — don't wait. Those are my top tips for your first week.
sentence_starters: First, show up [on time / early] — that means ...
Second, go over ... before your first day — this means ...
If a problem comes up, bring it up with ... right away.

writing_tasks.prompt: Write a short email from Ahmed to his team (80-100 words) about next week's schedule. Use at least 6 phrasal verbs from this lesson naturally in the email.
writing_tasks.example:
Subject: Next Week's Schedule and Updates

Hi team,

I wanted to bring up a few important points for next week. Please show up 15 minutes early on Monday for a brief orientation. I've set up a shared calendar — can you all fill out your availability by Thursday? Rosa will take over the inventory process and Marcus will help her go over the procedures. If any issues come up, please follow up with me directly — don't put off reporting problems.

Finally, hand in your timesheets by Friday noon.

Thanks,
Ahmed
rubric: Use at least 6 phrasal verbs from this lesson naturally in the text — not forced
Write a real workplace email format (subject line, greeting, body, sign-off)
Separate separable phrasal verbs correctly when using pronouns (fill it out, not fill out it)

writing_tasks.prompt: Write definitions and example sentences for all 8 phrasal verbs from this lesson. For each, write: 1) the phrasal verb, 2) its meaning in one sentence, 3) an example in a workplace context.
writing_tasks.example:
1. sort out — to resolve or organize a problem or situation.
Example: We need to sort out the delivery schedule before the client calls.

2. find out — to discover or learn information you didn't know.
Example: I found out that the shipment had been delayed by two days.

3. figure out — to understand or solve something through thinking.
Example: I'm trying to figure out why the inventory count doesn't match our records.

4. go over — to review or check something carefully.
Example: Let's go over the checklist before the inspection.

5. bring up — to mention a topic or issue in conversation.
Example: Ahmed brought up the staffing problem in the meeting.

6. follow up — to contact someone again to check on a previous matter.
Example: She followed up with the supplier three times before getting a response.

7. set up — to arrange or organize something.
Example: Can you set up a meeting for Thursday afternoon?

8. fill out — to complete a form by writing the required information.
Example: Please fill out the incident report before you leave today.
rubric: Define all 8 phrasal verbs — definition must capture the actual meaning, not just translate word for word
Each workplace example should use the verb naturally in a real sentence
Note whether each verb is separable or inseparable (e.g. 'fill it out' ✓ vs 'go over it' ✓ 'go it over' ✗)

grammar_focus.title: Separable vs Inseparable Phrasal Verbs
grammar_focus.explanation: Separable phrasal verbs allow the object between verb and particle; with pronouns it must go in the middle. Inseparable phrasal verbs keep the object after the full verb+particle.
examples: SEPARABLE: fill out the form / fill the form out / fill it out (pronoun must be in middle)
SEPARABLE: set up the meeting / set the meeting up / set it up
SEPARABLE: bring up the issue / bring the issue up / bring it up
INSEPARABLE: go over the report / go over it (NOT: go it over)
INSEPARABLE: find out the reason / find out about it (NOT: find it out)

grammar_focus.title: Pronoun Placement with Separable Phrasal Verbs
grammar_focus.explanation: When using a pronoun (it, them, him, her) with a separable phrasal verb, the pronoun MUST go between the verb and particle.
examples: Fill out the form → Fill it out ✓ (NOT: fill out it ✗)
Set up the meeting → Set it up ✓ (NOT: set up it ✗)
Bring up the issue → Bring it up ✓ (NOT: bring up it ✗)
Sort out the problem → Sort it out ✓ (NOT: sort out it ✗)
Figure out the answer → Figure it out ✓ (NOT: figure out it ✗)

practice.sentence: Can you set up the call? → Can you set ___ up?
I need to sort out the issue → I need to sort ___ out.
Ahmed brought up two concerns → Ahmed brought ___ up.

grammar_focus.title: Two Themes: Problem-solving and Workflow
grammar_focus.explanation: Grouping phrasal verbs by meaning helps you remember and use them. These 8 verbs fall into two clear workplace themes.
examples: PROBLEM-SOLVING: sort out (resolve), find out (discover), figure out (understand), go over (review)
WORKFLOW: bring up (raise), follow up (contact again), set up (arrange), fill out (complete a form)
Problem-solving example: I need to find out what caused the error and figure out a solution.
Workflow example: Can you set up a meeting so I can bring up the scheduling issue?
Combined: After you go over the report, follow up with me and we'll sort out any problems.

vocabulary.definition: resolve or organize a problem or situation
vocabulary.example: We need to sort out the scheduling conflict before Thursday.
I need to find out when the delivery is arriving.

vocabulary.definition: understand or solve something through thinking
vocabulary.example: I'm trying to figure out why the numbers don't match.
Let's go over the checklist before we start.

vocabulary.definition: raise or mention a topic in conversation
vocabulary.example: Please bring up any concerns at the meeting.

vocabulary.definition: contact someone again to check on a previous matter
vocabulary.example: I'll follow up with the supplier if we don't hear back.

vocabulary.definition: arrange or organize something (a meeting, system, process)
vocabulary.example: Can you set up a call for Thursday afternoon?

vocabulary.definition: complete a form or document by writing in the required information
vocabulary.example: You need to fill out this form to request time off.

vocabulary.definition: can be split apart; the object can go between verb and particle
vocabulary.example: Fill out is separable: fill it out.

vocabulary.definition: cannot be split; the object must follow the complete phrasal verb
vocabulary.example: Go over is inseparable: go over it (not go it over).

cultural_notes: Phrasal verbs are one of the most challenging aspects of English for non-native speakers because their meanings are often not predictable from the individual words.
Americans use phrasal verbs constantly in informal and semi-formal speech — knowing them is essential for sounding natural in workplace conversations.
In American workplace culture, knowing phrases like 'follow up', 'sort out', and 'bring up' is especially important for professional communication and meetings.

Some phrasal verbs have formal equivalents: 'resolve' sounds more formal than 'sort out', 'discover' is more formal than 'find out' — but the phrasal verbs feel more natural in everyday American workplace speech.

Phrasal verbs often appear in American business idioms and email subject lines: 'Following up on...', 'Checking in on...', 'Circling back on...' are extremely common in American professional email culture.
